subtopic: STATEMENT ON ACCIDENT TO UNITED STATES AIR FORCE PLANE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON ACCIDENT TO UNITED STATES AIR FORCE PLANE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I promised the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that I would make a statement today with respect to the incident which occurred at Mount Hope airport near Hamilton on Tuesday last.
About 1.30 in the afternoon a United States air force Cl24 Globemaster, carrying a crew of 15 in addition to 81 United States air force servicemen as passengers, made an emergency landing at the Royal Canadian Air Force station, Mount Hope. While en route from a base in Ohio to a base in Newfoundland, the aircraft developed gasoline leakage in its starboard wing. Efforts to stop the leakage failed and, because of the serious fire risk, the pilot stopped the two starboard engines. Inability
to maintain altitude, a continuing fire hazard and weather limitations at other airfields in the vicinity led the pilot to select Mount Hope for an emergency landing.
During the approach to the airfield attempts to lower the undercarriage failed and the pilot correctly decided to carry out a wheels-up landing in a grass area clear of the concrete runways. This he skilfully accomplished without injury to any of the 96 servicemen aboard, who hastily evacuated the aircraft, some carrying the arms which were part of their service equipment.
Spectators quickly gathered and soon included press reporters and photographers. Only a small detachment of Royal Canadian Air Force personnel was available and Squadron Leader C. A. Bayley, officer commanding at Mount Hope, immediately conferred with the captain of the Globemaster and arranged that the small R.C.A.F. detachment would endeavour to control access to and from the airfield and that the U.S. air force members would stand guard over the aircraft. The aircraft was still carrying 4,000 gallons of gasoline which was leaking from the plane, and there was extreme danger that the escaping fumes would become ignited by electrical shorts, flash bulbs or sparks from some other cause. For this reason no U.S.A.F. or any other personnel were permitted to come near the damaged aircraft for two and a half hours after the crash landing. In the course of carrying out their duties the guards restrained all persons from approaching closer than approximately 50 yards, explaining to them the great danger of fire. Photographers were permitted to take photographs of the aircraft from beyond this distance.
News reporters who requested information from the guards were asked to proceed to the entrance office where Squadron Leader Bayley and the captain of the aircraft would endeavour to answer their inquiries. Those newsmen who availed themselves of this opportunity later expressed their satisfaction for the co-operation thus extended.
One small group of three news photographers, unobserved by the guard, came closer than 50 yards before they were seen. They were told that they could take photographs but not closer than 50 yards because of the fire hazard. They were also told of the facilities arranged to provide information.
The news photographers then withdrew, but one of them again came forward and was

Inquiries of the Ministry asked to move back by Lieutenant Davis, U.S. Air Force, who was in fact third pilot during the emergency landing. This news photographer, Godfrey Scott, ignored the request, whereupon the officer drew his revolver and, although not pointing it at anyone, again warned the photographer not to come any closer. After some words Mr. Scott asked the lieutenant to put his revolver away. This he did, and the photographer then withdrew, having in the meantime, I think, taken a picture.
Shortly after this incident, some news photographers and/or newsmen asked a U.S.A.F. sergeant, who had his rifle slung over his shoulder, if he would unsling his rifle and hold it in his hands in front of him to be photographed. This request was complied with, the sergeant explaining as he did so that the rifle was not loaded. It was this photograph which appeared on the front page of yesterday morning's Globe and Mail, and I am told that it was pictures of this sergeant and his rifle which appeared in the television news Tuesday evening and again last night. Hon. members can form their own opinion of posed pictures under such circumstances.

subsubtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 214, to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when the Trans-Canada Highway Act became law on December 10, 1949, it was our hope that within seven years of that date there would be a good all-weather transcontinental road in Canada. When nine of the ten provincial governments subsequently signed agreements with the federal government we had good reason to anticipate that by the end of this current year, that is, by the end of 1956, Canada would at least have a high standard paved highway from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Victoria, British Columbia, along the shortest practical route.
I do not believe there were many people then who felt we were guilty of overoptimism. After all, Canadian history contains many illustrations of our ability to bridge our great spaces in the interests of transportation and communication.
It is interesting in fact to look back to the nineteenth century when Canadians were engaged in spanning Canada by rail. That was a lamplit horse-and-buggy era, and there were far less conveniences and construction tools to work with than we have today. Yet it took just eight years to link Quebec to the Atlantic seaboard by rail after the route was finally selected and managers were appointed in 1868, and it took just 11 years to push the C.P.R. through to the Pacific despite
3068	HOUSE OF
Trans-Canada Highway Act acrimonious disputes, scandal, lethargic progress for a time, absence of human settlement and tremendous obstacles in the land itself.
The bill now before the house would extend the term for building the trans-Canada highway from seven years to 11 years, which is the same time it took nineteenth century Canada to build the C.P.R. The future of the west and of Canada itself was at stake in those days. There has apparently not been anything like the same sense of urgency to goad this new highway building project, but there thas been for some years a sense of national awareness that a country of this size and importance should have a coast-to-coast highway; that our people should be able, in this automotive era, to drive in comfort from Newfoundland to British Columbia on Canadian soil.
This feeling had actually provoked a number of attempts to build such a road before 1949, the last being in 1930 when the federal government undertook to pay part of the cost to help cope with unemployment. I find upon review that from 1931 to 1941 about $45 million was paid to the provinces for road-building projects, which helped to eliminate the unemployment prevailing during that period. This 1930 effort did assist in the construction of additional highway mileage but it fell far short of the objective and the concept of a coast-to-coast highway remained a hope for the future.
It remained for the second world war and the buoyant post-war period to give new emphasis to the need for a trans-Canada highway. When Newfoundland entered confederation in 1949, there was a new concept of enabling vehicle traffic to flow with comparative ease-not from Nova Scotia but from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Victoria, British Columbia. Newfoundland needed a paved trans-island highway of its own and its need fitted into this broader picture that Canada has been contemplating.
I may say here that in building roads there is a matter of jurisdiction which the federal government and all the provincial governments have always had clearly in mind. In this, as in all matters, the federal government has no wish to invade the jurisdiction of the other levels of government. Roads are normally considered to be the direct concern of the provincial governments. It seemed clear, however, that most provinces were anxious for federal financial participation but it has never been responsibly suggested that the provinces should surrender their initiative or their position under the constitution with respect to roads.
If the project were to go forward there seemed to be a need for co-ordination which


appeared to be a valid role for the federal government. Moreover the road would have a national character. It would help to weld the country more closely together and it would also, we felt, contribute to national growth and development just as the railways did in the nineteenth century and as other major transportation projects in various fields have done since.
Having regard to these factors and to what we considered to be the wishes of the public, the federal government in 1948 invited all ten provincial governments to participate in discussions to determine how to give Canada one long main street as quickly as possible.
Committees were set up to recommend standards, routes, completion dates and so forth. Neither the federal government nor the provinces laid down any one-way rules or standards. It was a matter of amicable discussions and mutual understandings. It was agreed that the portion of the highway across each province would be built by the provincial government concerned, that it would remain the property of the provincial government and be maintained by it with no disturbance whatever to its own sovereign jurisdiction and that the road when completed would conform to the standards mutually decided upon.
We agreed in 1949 that if parliament approved, the federal government would make contributions to a provincial government of 50 per cent of the construction costs of the highway over a seven-year period. Moreover the federal government undertook to contribute up to one-half of the cost of a highway constructed prior to the date of the act and which could qualify for inclusion in the trans-Canada highway.
That was the formula which we brought before parliament in 1949 in the form of a bill which was enacted more than six years ago as the Trans-Canada Highway Act. It provided, amongst other things, for an amount of $150 million for the federal share of half the anticipated over-all cost of construction. Under the authority of the act federal-provincial agreements were prepared which provided for federal financial contributions, terms and conditions for inviting tenders, methods of determining the cost of new and prior construction, routes, standards and inspection. Within six months, eight of the provincial governments had signed agreements to build their portion of the highway by December 9, 1956. By May, 1952, nine of the ten provinces had become signatories.
Exclusive of the province of Quebec, the length of the trans-Canada highway is 4,497 miles in the provinces and 83 miles in the national parks, a total of 4,580 miles in all.

Of this distance approximately 2,850 miles are now paved although the equivalent of only 1,600 miles, or 35 per cent, has been constructed to trans-Canada standards. Thus there remain approximately 1,545 miles of unpaved highway and there still are physical gaps totalling about 185 miles where there is no highway of any kind.
Broken down by provinces, the length of the highway together with the distances now paved, the equivalent mileages that have
Trans-Canada Highway Act been constructed to trans-Canada highway standards, together with the distances for which there is no highway of any kind, are tabulated as follows, and with the permission of the house I should like to place this table on Hansard.

As to the 83 miles in the national parks, while this is not included in the terms of the agreement, the federal government has been making progress toward completing this mileage under some of the most difficult conditions of construction encountered anywhere in Canada. Hon. members are aware, I am sure, that to date the trans-Canada highway in the national parks is in Banff and Yoho where the mountainous conditions make road building very difficult. We aim, however, to have the work completed within the time specified in the bill now before you.
On the basis of progress to date it seems clear that in no province will the trans-Canada highway be completed by December 9, 1956, the expiration date of the present federal-provincial agreement. There are various reasons advanced by the provincial governments-many of them valid and justifiable-for the construction lag, such as a shortage of engineers, weather, the Korean war, great physical obstacles imposed by all sorts of topographical handicaps, the urgent 67509-194J
demands for highways in areas not covered by the national route, and others. But in the main progress has been disappointingly slow despite periodic conferences and efforts to accelerate the work. Consequently it has been necessary once again to review the whole operation and to recommend to parliament additional steps calculated to hasten the realization of this long-awaited project.
Now, if the federal government is to provide a further incentive to the provincial governments, it would seem evident that priority should be given to highway construction in those areas where no highway exists at the present time. The first objective then, I feel, should be the elimination of these gaps and the linking of the various completed sections to form a continuous route. A study of the road has revealed that in no province do the gaps exceed 10 per cent of the total mileage of the route within that province's boundaries. In fact, most provinces now have a continuous road although many sections may not conform to
3070	HOUSE OF
Trans-Canada Highway Act trans-Canada highway standards. The main incentive therefore in the bill now before hon. members is to close the existing gaps.
Now as to road already paved, I feel it would be unrealistic for a province to tear up a reasonably good existing paved highway merely for the purpose of rebuilding it to trans-Canada highway standards. There is no suggestion here that we should depart from the agreed standards when new construction or reconstruction is involved. High standard highways for modern vehicle traffic are a necessary and sound investment. I believe, therefore, that the aim should be to construct as much mileage to the agreed standards as is within the capacity of each provincial government. However, there is no good reason why an adequately paved road, even if slightly below trans-Canada highway standards, should not be used until its normal life has been exhausted unless, of course, traffic requirements demand a higher standard of highway now.
It has been suggested that federal contributions should be increased above the present level of 50 per cent. In fairness to those provinces which have made the greatest progress, any general or over-all increase beyond 50 per cent would have to be retroactive to the dates upon which the federal-provincial agreements were signed. Retroactive legislation of this nature gives rise to many problems and moreover I have serious doubts as to whether this approach would achieve the desired end. Further, no advantage would be gained if the federal government increased its contributions only to have the provincial governments reduce expenditures on the highway by a similar amount. What is required is an increased effort on the part of all concerned.
To discuss ways and means to accelerate the pace of work on the trans-Canada highway, we invited all provincial ministers concerned to attend, with their officials, a conference in Ottawa last November. This conference was again characterized by a harmonious and constructive approach to the problem and a mutual desire to complete the project. At that time I outlined some of the suggestions the federal government was prepared to incorporate into legislation to be placed before parliament if the participating provinces so wished. While some of the provincial ministers expressed the hope that we might have gone further, I believe they all felt that the approach we suggested was reasonable and that it would go a long way towards achieving a completed highway.
Following the conference, the officials of the trans-Canada highway division of the Department of Public Works visited and discussed with officials of the participating


provinces matters of detail and various engineering approaches. As a result of the conference and these subsequent discussions, we were able to draft the bill which is now before you and, moreover, we have prepared draft agreements which are now in the hands of the various provincial highway ministers for their consideration, so that no time will be lost in starting work under this new formula if and when the legislation is approved by parliament.
With the foregoing considerations in mind, I wish to turn to the four proposed amendments to the act contained in this bill. Since it seems certain that additional time will be required for the completion of the highway, one amendment contemplates the extension of the construction period to December 31, 1960. This will permit four additional construction seasons over and above those now authorized by the act, or five full construction seasons from this date. A further five months will be provided to wind up the accounting. The termination date for all federal contributions, therefore, would be set at May 31, 1961.
I might say here that the termination date for construction, December 31, 1960, was a matter of virtually mutual agreement. For the benefit of those hon. members who have said that the provinces simply cannot complete the highway by that date, I would say that the provinces themselves say they can. At the conference I suggested a termination date of December 31, 1959. Some but not all of the provinces thought that was a bit tight. I thereupon asked their wishes individually and it was they who said they thought they could complete the job if they were given one year longer, and they recommended a target date of December 31, 1960. We met the wishes of the provincial governments in this respect.
I have mentioned that in no province is there more than 10 per cent of the total mileage where no highway exists at the present time. On the other hand, there is one province that has little more than 10 per cent of its total mileage left to complete and some others are pretty well advanced. As an incentive to closing these remaining gaps, the bill contains an amendment which would authorize the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to increase the scale of contributions to a province for highway construction on the route, with the higher payments limited to 10 per cent of the provincial mileage.
The proposed formula will provide for the payment of 90 per cent of the construction costs of one-tenth of the total mileage in each province and 50 per cent of the other nine-tenths whereas at present the act limits the federal government to 50 per cent of the cost of construction of all the mileage along the

In other words, what we are now looking for is an extra effort.
For other portions of the highway the basis of sharing costs will remain as at present, which is that the federal government will contribute 50 per cent of the costs of new and prior construction. Under the act the provision for prior construction remains in
Trans-Canada Highway Act force for a seven year period expiring December 9, 1956. This prior construction period dates from April 1, 1928, and in practice severe problems have been encountered in establishing a realistic basis for evaluating construction carried out over such a long period prior to the passing of the act. These difficulties have been disproportionate to the amount of funds involved and in most cases the determination of value has been at best a fair estimate. This whole matter has been discussed with the provincial governments, and having regard to the circumstances I have mentioned and the fact that the prior construction clause would in any event elapse on the expiry date of the present act, it is not intended to continue this provision beyond the agreed date of December 9, 1956. An amendment is included accordingly.
I might mention here that during the November conference the question of the federal government's policy of contributions to the construction of cloverleafs and similar type intersections was discussed at some length. Canada has been sharing the construction costs incurred within 50 feet on each side of the centre line of the trans-Canada highway. That is the 100 foot right of way contemplated by the agreement. As a result of discussions at the conference, a thorough review of this question was made and we have now agreed to broaden federal participation. In addition to contributions with respect to construction costs along the trans-Canada highway, including a grade separation structure, the federal government will participate in costs incurred on ramps or connecting legs within the limits of the intersection. The principle is that facilities such as these ramps or connections should be of equal value to each intersecting highway. The cost of providing them will be apportioned between the two roads and will have regard to the proportion of the total cost that is borne by the provincial government. There is a wide variety of designs of grade separations and each new one will be considered separately to see how the revised basis of sharing costs will apply.

These two factors have necessitated a revision in estimates and it is now anticipated that the federal government's share of the costs of construction will amount to $250 million. Accordingly, the bill seeks authorization of an increase in the total federal government expenditure from $150 million to $250 million.
In summary, the bill to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act proposes these four major amendments:
(1)	The extension of the highway construction period to December 31, 1960, with federal contributions terminating May 31, 1961.
(2)	An increase in the federal government's contribution to include 90 per cent of the construction costs on one-tenth of the total mileage in each province, such contributions to apply only to work done after this agreement is signed pursuant to the bill now before us.
(3)	The termination of federal contributions for prior highway construction, as of the previously agreed date of December 9, 1956. There is no change there as far as the present statute is concerned.
(4)	An increase from $150 million to $250 million in the amount which the federal government may contribute towards the costs of highway construction.
I believe that the proposed amendments to the act will have the effect of accelerating the rate of construction and I sincerely hope that by the end of 1960 our goal of a trans-Canada highway will be realized.

No, the minister is speaking while I am still on my feet. I think the minister would have done better not to mention a comparison between the 11 years it took to build the Canadian Pacific Railway and the 11 years that he says it is now going to take to build the trans-Canada highway. After all, the Canadian Pacific Railway was built at a time when the line had to be put through many sections of the country that had not been traversed. The kind of equipment that was available for building railways or roads in that day was much less efficient than is the modern road building machinery we now possess. The railway had to be built where there were no roads before the Canadian Pacific tracks were put down. This highway is being built in many places by improving roads that are already there; at least it is being built in areas where we already have roads of some sort.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that by this reference to nineteenth century history the minister has simply highlighted the fact that the present project is being proceeded with at a snail's pace for the times in which we are living.

I know, of course, that when the government wants to boast of anything that has been accomplished, even if it is a 30 per cent accomplishment, it is of course because of what the federal government has done. On the other hand if there are complaints made because things have not been accomplished the federal government blames the provinces for that lack of accomplishment.
As has already been expressed by my colleagues speaking on our behalf, we contend that the main reason for the slowness with which this highway is being built is because the federal government has not yet recognized its national character and the fact that federal financial responsibility should be much greater than has been set out in the
3078	HOUSE OF
Trans-Canada Highway Act legislation that is now on the statute books. It should be greater than that which the legislation provides as amended by the bill which is now before us.
Up to the present time the arrangement has been for the federal treasury to pay 50 per cent of the cost of constructing the highway without any participation by the federal government in the maintenance of the highway after it is built. This interesting formula that we now have, whereby the federal government will contribute 90 per cent of the cost of 10 per cent of the highway, seems to add up, if my arithmetic is correct, to what amounts to 54 per cent of the total cost of the highway in the provinces. I arrive at that figure by taking 50 per cent of 90 per cent, which amounts to 45 per cent, and then I take 90 per cent of 10 per cent of the highway, which is 9 per cent, and by adding 45 per cent and 9 per cent one gets a total of 54 per cent. That is still a long way short of the figure of 75 per cent which is what we feel the federal government should be doing by way of participation in the cost of a national project such as the trans-Canada highway.
Frankly we feel that the fact that the government has fallen down on the financial aspect of this matter is the main reason that in the twentieth century it is taking just as long to build the trans-Canada highway as it took in the nineteenth century to build the Canadian Pacific railway.
We feel that there is still a tremendous lack of vision on the part of the federal government as to the possibility of uniting this country more closely, as to the possibility of development both in economic terms and in terms of tourist traffic, and also in getting our people to move about and know better all parts of Canada. We feel that with respect to all this the government has not yet caught the vision which is shared by a great many people in this country. We still call upon the government to catch that vision and to translate it into a greater federal financial participation in the trans-Canada highway.
It seems to me that another indication of the lack of vision on the part of the federal government is the fact that there is a cut-off date in the present legislation, and that a cut-off date will still be in the act as amended even though it is advanced to December 31, 1960, with one more year to clean up the accounts. That is the attitude which the federal government takes towards the trans-Canada highway, toward a national highway program. It has not really got into this program with both feet, it has got into it temporarily and it envisions the day when 

this act will be spent and the federal government will have no more responsibility. When this point was raised the other day the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Public Works accepted that implication by saying that once this project is completed, the highway in the various provinces will be the property of the provinces; in other words, the federal government responsibility would be finished. I say that is the mark of the attitude of the government toward this whole program and it is certainly one of a lack of vision.
The provinces have to concern themselves, not only with finding their percentage of the cost of building the highway; they have to concern themselves also with acquiring the necessary land and then they must think of the costs of maintenance after the highway is built, not only during the period of time when this act will be in effect but after the act has been spent and the federal government has bowed out of the picture. On top of all that, the provinces must concern themselves with their other highway programs, so that when you survey the whole picture the fact of the matter is that what the federal government is doing is really very little compared with the responsibility of the provinces and compared with the important part that a well planned national highway program could play in the development of this country.
As has been indicated in previous debates, we feel that there should be not just one trans-Canada highway but a second transcontinental road, and also highways running north and south connecting with highways that come up to the border from the United States. Indeed we feel that any government with vision regarding this matter would have a total, over-all program that would involve a formula for federal financial participation in the various road programs of the provinces of this country.
We in this House of Commons today find ourselves in the position of having to support what is offered to us because it constitutes some improvement. We cannot vote against it; we have to accept it if we want the program accelerated. This legislation does that to a certain extent and therefore we must vote for it. But we know that once this legislation has been passed the government will do nothing until some crisis develops later on or until some government with vision sits to the right of Your Honour.
A few days ago I happened to be standing in the main central hall of this building waiting for a friend. While waiting I read once again the inscription which appears on the main centre column in the lobby in the central

part of this parliament building. Although I have read it before I was struck forcibly by what it said when, I read it again. It refers to the fact that on July 1, 1917, this building was dedicated in memory of those who gave their lives in the first world war. That was done, as the inscription says, on the fiftieth anniversary of confederation.
What struck me rather forcibly was that that date, which in the lives of most of us who are here seems so recent, July 1, 1917, was the date on which this country was celebrating its fiftieth anniversary. I realized as I have done before, because I have had a resolution on the order paper suggesting this, that already we are much closer to the one hundredth anniversary of the birth of this country than we are to that fiftieth anniversary. A little more than 11 years from now we shall be celebrating Canada's one hundredth birthday.
When that time comes I hope we will be celebrating it with something more than fireworks and speeches and programs over the radio and television. I hope we will have achieved some really noteworthy signs of development in this country. There are many fields in which we could really launch a gigantic program of development so that we could have a birthday which could be celebrated proudly on July 1, 1967. I suggest to the Minister of Public Works that several of these fields are in his department-I think of fields such as housing-and that the one we are dealing with today, the trans-Canada highway, offers such a field, as would a national highway program. I hope that by July 1, 1967, we will have, not just a Liberal government still trying to complete the first trans-Canada highway but a vast program of highways connecting all parts of this country, adding to the economic development of Canada and making it possible for our people to travel about with ease and comfort on good highways.
That will be accomplished only if in the years that are with us right now, not ten or twenty years from now but in the years in which we are working right now, the government catches the vision of this project and brings before parliament an adequate highway program.
Parliament can do no other than to support the bill which is before us today as it accelerates the construction of the one highway that is now under construction. But it is only a piecemeal solution. I hope the government will rethink the whole question of its financial responsibility in relation to our highway program and bring down with the least possible delay a plan that will make possible
Trans-Canada Highway Act the building of a network of roads and highways in this country such as this country can support and such as the people of Canada deserve.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the bill on this occasion. When we were discussing the resolution the other day I made some general remarks, but there are one or two other things I should like to draw to the minister's attention. In the first place, I am quite sure that the minister would be the last person in the house to say that he was satisfied with the progress that this development has been making. Certainly after five years the progress that has been made in the development of the trans-Canada highway is a disgrace, and I think the minister agrees with that. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I think the minister would be in very bad taste if he were to criticize the provinces too much because, as has already been indicated this afternoon, the federal government has set an exceedingly poor example on that portion of the trans-Canada highway which they have to build.
It is true, as the minister suggested when making his remarks a while ago, that the work which the federal government has to do in the national parks is possibly a little different from some of the other construction work throughout the provinces. But do not let anybody be misled about the matter. There are sections in the national parks that can be constructed more easily than sections of the road in the prairie provinces or in the province of British Columbia.
For instance, let me give the minister one stretch by way of example, the 8 miles running from the east gate of Banff park to two miles east of the town of Banff just before you cross the river. That was one of the easiest sections in all Canada to build a road. After the bush was cleared, which was not a major problem under present day methods of removing bush, a solid gravel bed was found and there was practically no gravel to haul at all. What little gravel they did haul for the base was obtained from a mountain right at the side of the road. Yet after five years that 8 miles of road is not even completed. Indeed, not only is it not completed but they have not even got a road with a good base. The minister knows that is so because, according to the answer given the other day to a question of mine, we are spending $200 to $300 a mile for repairs.
The present asphalt-bound 9-inch gravel base is all going to pieces and it is only a short period of time since it was constructed.
3080	HOUSE OF
Trans-Canada Highway Act The minister can say if he wishes that when the hard surface is laid it will protect the road, but it will do no such thing. In the province of Alberta we are endeavouring to leave our hard surface roads without the final top coat for two or three years in order to see if they will stand up, and wherever we find a place where the road does not stand up the material is removed all the way down and a new sub-grade is put in. We .find it is cheaper to do that than it is to put on the final coat, then find that there are defects underneath and have to tear up the whole thing.
Let us not get the idea that just because the government section runs through the national parks which are part mountainous all of the road being constructed there is in mountainous terrain. It is not. I am not belittling for a minute the difficulties that one finds in the construction of highways, but after five years' work surely the government should have at least 8 miles finished. Instead the program now calls for 11 years and unless the federal government gets a real move on they will not even have it finished in that 11 year period because there is still a tremendous amount of work to do in the national parks.
While the minister was speaking I could not help but wonder if this is really a trans-Canada highway. What efforts is the minister putting forth to see that it becomes such? There is one province in the dominion that is not taking any part in the construction of the trans-Canada highway. I think that is bad from the point of view of both provincial and federal relations. I should like to see the minister do something about this matter and try to see if he cannot get the province of Quebec to co-operate a little more with the rest of Canada in the construction of the trans-Canada highway so that people will be able to travel from one coast of Canada to the other on a trans-Canada highway. They will not be able to do so unless the minister can induce the province of Quebec to assume its share in the building of the trans-Canada highway.
That brings up another point. What is the purpose of a trans-Canada highway? I noticed when the minister was speaking, and I am not disagreeing with what he said particularly, that he wanted a road so that people would be able to travel across Canada and enjoy themselves. I hope they will. That is one purpose but it is only one of the purposes. The minister wants the road to attract tourists and assist our tourist trade. It is nice to have a film in colour showing the beautiful


scenery along the highway and the rapidity with which it is being constructed, if that is so.

Part of it will have to be in slow motion. That is certain. But, Mr. Speaker, in my judgment there is another purpose of a trans-Canada highway. I think the trans-Canada highway should be built not only to attract tourists and give them pleasure but for the purpose of transporting goods and passengers. I make no apology for saying that then we will have a trans-Canada highway that will provide competition for our railway system. We in western Canada have hopes that that is what the road will be used for because that will be the only form of competition for our two national railway systems.
Every time there is a boost in freight rates we in the west and the people of the mari-times as well have to bear the brunt of it. That condition should not be allowed to continue. Therefore I am going to take a few minutes to speak about the specifications of the trans-Canada highway. When I was speaking the other day about this matter the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) interrupted me and said, as found at page 2951 of Hansard of April 16:
The trans-Canada highway is still the best-
I replied, "No, it is not." I will agree that the specifications of the trans-Canada highway were probably the best until about a year or two ago. I think that statement is quite correct. When the trans-Canada highway specifications were first drawn up they were a good set of specifications compared with those applying to other roads then being built. This is why I particularly want to draw the attention of the house now to the fact that this highway should not be built solely to attract tourists and for the pleasure of tourists but should also be built to carry heavy freight traffic. Of course the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys was endeavouring to imply that the trans-Canada highway specifications were far above the specifications of provincial highways in Alberta. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) has drawn my attention to the fact that the minister was referring particularly to Alberta. But we should not be concerned whether the specifications are equal to those of the provinces because the financial ability of the provinces enters into the picture. As has been pointed out this afternoon, the provinces are finding difficulty in carrying out their share of this program because of the question of finances, but the federal government has not got that reason to fall back on. We

should be giving every attention to improving the specifications, especially when it has been so clearly pointed out in all parts of this continent that present road structures are not strong enough to carry the traffic required today. I think the minister made reference to this matter when he was speaking. I could not hear him very well because there was some conversation going on around here. Hence if I am not interpreting him correctly, I am sure he will correct me. I thought he said that some mention had been made about the specifications but that this was a little bit late to do it.

I want to compare some of the specifications of the trans-Canada highway with the specifications in the province of Alberta where they have found out that the present specifications as applying to the trans-Canada highway just will not bear the traffic. I want to give some of the instances where the Alberta grading specifications exceed the federal trans-Canada highway specifications.
We have highway No. 2 which runs from Airdrie to Crossfield. That is a highway with four 12-foot lanes. May I say right here that the minister will recall my saying, I am sure, when we were first talking about the trans-Canada highway. I then suggested to him that we should build a four-lane trans-Canada highway, and that if we could not see our way clear to build the four lanes at present, we should at least buy the right of way so that we could extend the road when it became necessary from two lanes to four lanes. He now tells us, I think, that the specifications call for a 100-foot right of way. Of course a 100-foot right of way will not provide for a four-lane highway with a medium in between, as there should be. In fact, a 100-foot right of way will not be sufficient to build a proper four-lane highway with proper drainage on each side, even without a midway. It seems to me that that is negligence of the highest degree when we are speaking about a national highway.
The No. 2 highway running from Airdrie to Crossfield is a highway with four 12-foot lanes, divided with a 30-foot medium and 10-foot shoulders. That far exceeds anything that the trans-Canada highway has. Then highway No. 2 from Crossfield to Bowden is one with four 12-foot lanes, with a 20-foot medium and 10-foot shoulders. Highway No. 2 running from Aldersyde to High River is one with four 12-foot lanes, undivided, with 12-foot shoulders. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to notice this about all these highways that I have mentioned. They are of

Yes. That
provision was made in order to comply with the specifications in certain provinces. In our province those shoulders are asphalt, but in large sections of Ontario they are not. Although I stand subject to correction on this point, I do not believe there are any 10-foot shoulders on the trans-Canada highway in Ontario that are asphalt. We have a 14-inch stabilized base course against the trans-Canada highway 9-inch base course. But we are not even satisfied that that is going to stand the strain. Then on those highways that I have mentioned we have a 4-inch asphaltic surface course whereas the trans-Canada highway has a 3-inch asphaltic surface course; and that makes a tremendous difference.
We have other four-lane undivided highways, Mr. Speaker. The ones I have mentioned were divided highways. While I am speaking about these highways may I say also that I suggested to the minister when I was speaking the other day-and I am going to repeat this point because I am afraid the minister was not in the chamber just at the moment when I was speaking about it- that surely we should make all our trans-Canada highways which lead into the cities four-lane highways at least 20 miles outside these cities. Not only in the province of Alberta but in every large city across Canada it is found that wherever the trans-Canada highway or any main highway goes into the city traffic is so terrifically heavy, at least within 20 miles of the city border, that two lanes will never handle it. As one particular instance I point out the road between Calgary and Banff on holidays. The traffic is terrific there and it is a dangerous hazard that should not be permitted. That road is yet to be constructed. They are surveying that portion, about 85 miles in length. Now is the time to make it a four-lane highway. Now is the time to raise the specifications. The freight which goes between Alberta and British Columbia will be obliged to go over that section between Calgary and British Columbia because there is no other trans-Canada highway across the mountains. Those specifications will never carry the traffic.


The minister may say that as far as four lanes are concerned there is no provision in the regulations to allow of the construction of four lanes on any portion of the trans-Canada highway. In reply I would say this. We are now revising this act. Now is the time to make those -conditions available to the provinces.
Let me give you the names of these other roads which are undivided: From Edmonton to Nisku; from Calgary to Airdrie; from Calgary to Aldersyde. Then we have in addition highway No. 11, the road which runs from Sylvan Lake to Condor. That has a 12-inch minimum stabilized base course, which is 3 inches more than the trans-Canada highway. Then we have highway No. 12 going from Stettler to Gadsby, highway No. 16 going from Pedley to Jasper park and highway No. 43 from Gunn to Cherhill and Whitecourt to Valleyview. It is all four-inch asphaltic surface course with twelve-inch base being used on these projects.
This is in the province of Alberta. I am sure other provinces can speak for themselves and that they have much the same story, but we are finding without any qualification that the present standards of the trans-Canada highway will never stand up to the traffic unless we are going to bar trucks from using it, and that is what I fear. Make no mistake about it. I never expected to be a prophet, but you do not have to get into the field of prophecy to foresee that, and I am looking at the Minister of Transport right now.

We should take precautions in this regard. I said a moment ago we in Alberta were not even satisfied with the superior qualifications of the Alberta highway, and so we are carrying on tests in that province. We have a test mile north of Calgary on highway 2. It is non-divided with four lanes, with eight-foot asphalt bound shoulders. There are two sections in this test, each one mile long. One is the concrete section, which is a six-inch stabilized base and eight-inch unreinforced concrete. I do not know of a section of road in Canada that betters that. Then the asphalt section is an 18-inch stabilized base course-that is twice the base course of the trans-Canada highway-with a four-inch asphaltic surface course, with, 10-foot gravel shoulders and asphalt bound. These roads are built right in the highway No. 2 coming down from Edmonton to Calgary so that all the traffic which goes over that main highway No. 2 has to go over these two test strips. If it is found that those two sections wall bear the traffic better than the others, then of course

we shall have to begin improving the already improved roads that we have now.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be accused by the Chair of repetition, and I do not want my conscience to bother me after I sit down to the extent that it will say to me, "You should have said this and you did not." I want to be able to say to the minister later on, if this road does not hold up, "Well, I told you so." That will be poor consolation for either me or the minister. I am not saying this to be critical of him, because I have always found him to be a very reasonable minister, but I say to him that he should have a second look at these specifications.

I have just a brief word to say about the leadership of the present minister. He showed today the leadership that he is capable of giving and has been giving, in the statement that he made before us today. This statement will read well. He told us early in the statement how, with his officials and the ministers of highways of the provinces, he held a conference. They came to their plan of how that highway should be built, and the provinces would do the work and the dominion government would pay 50 per cent of the cost. Is that not right?
Therefore, the leadership that the present minister had to give during those years was to see that his 50 per cent was paid. I shall ask the minister, "Is there any other type of leadership you are asked to give?" Fifty per cent of the leadership to the provinces and no more. I do not know one case where that 50 per cent of the cost was not paid, except in Fort William, and I commend him for holding back the money when some officials disgraced their provincial government. I would say that the premier of Ontario did a fine job in cleaning that up, and I pay my tribute to him.
The present leadership could not be better. Every dollar that was needed from the dominion government was paid. What more could he do? He could not interfere with the provincial government. I am not going to use the words describing the leadership
Trans-Canada Highway Act of the minister; it is not necessary. But it was honest, it was fair, it was just and it was reasonable.
What has happened in the second place? The provincial ministers and their officials and the dominion government with its ministers and officials held another conference. They agreed on the present bill. What leadership has the minister to give to see that that bill is carried out? He should give the leadership that he is capable of giving and see that the money is paid and nothing else. He has no business to interfere in the construction of the highway. I will admit that sometimes I get criticized in Fort William for not trying to see that the dominion government had something to say in the building of that highway. I want to see the highway go ahead, and I want to see this bill accelerated. I do not intend to take 40 minutes, and I shall end in about half a minute. We want to see this highway built because it will show to the rest of Canada one of the beauty spots of Canada: Fort William. You will see something there. That highway into Fort William is good.
There have been those who have said that we should have a road north and south. Our provincial government-and I pay this tribute to it-has just as good a road from Fort William to Pigeon river as there is on the other side, and the tourists from the United States tell us that. We want this highway because there is so much to see in Fort William and Port Arthur-the finest scenery in Canada, bar none. Therefore, I shall close by saying to the minister, "Just carry on, do what you usually do, do not try to take the chip off the other fellow's shoulders, just wink at him and tell him to go ahead, have your say, and be a good boy."

Mr. Speaker, I am sure Your Honour will not chastise me for being repetitious, since this is the first time I have spoken either on this bill or at the resolution stage. It would seem to me that the federal government has been taking its responsibilities too lightly in the past to be prepared to be more active in the future in adding its contribution to a national road. At this time I should like to quote a paragraph from the "Canadian Tax Foundation":

I am speaking specifically now of my own province of Ontario. We have in the south an abundance of population which is calling for roads and more roads, and it is impossible for the government of Ontario, as well as the governments of other provinces, to contribute their 50 per cent of the cost of the trans-Canada highway and still build and maintain the roads which they must build and maintain in the southern part of the province. At this time I should like to draw the minister's attention to the tremendous number of vehicular miles travelled in the province of Ontario and the increase that is expected in the next 10 years. It was estimated that 13 billion miles were travelled in the province of Ontario in the past year, and that in 1965 some 25 billion miles will be travelled by vehicles. That brings out most forcibly the contributions the different provinces must make in fulfilling their duties to their own people. We must admit, Mr. Speaker, that this transcontinental highway is not what we might call a provincial road; it is interprovincial. It is even more than that; it is international in its aspects and as such I contend, Mr. Speaker, that the federal Liberal government is not contributing its share. It is not contributing what it should to build this road speedily so that traffic can travel from east to west and from west to east.
At the present time we can visualize the tremendous number of Canadian tourists who go from east to west and from west to east over the United States highway system. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just stated that he hopes when in 1967 we celebrate the centenary of confederation we shall be able to celebrate it by the residents of Canada being in a position to travel over this trans-Canada highway from east to west and west to east and thereby gain a fuller knowledge of what Canada is. But I am afraid that if progress is not any speedier in the next five years than it has been jn the past five we shall not have that privilege.
I must say that the responsibility of the provinces to their own residents is tremendous. The governments of the provinces are contributing not only 100 per cent of highway costs in their respective provinces, but they are also contributing tremendously to municipal and county roads. I will give an


illustration of that. In the year 1954 the Ontario government contributed to our municipal and county roads the sum of $32,787,000. In 1955 it is estimated that they contributed $41 million. That figure will have to be increased, because the municipalities have gone practically to the limit in financing schools, roads and so forth, and the government must come to their rescue and contribute a greater proportion of the cost.
It is up to the dominion government to cease its mollycoddling way of doing things, which it has been using in the past five years. Let it contribute 75 per cent, 80 per cent or even 90 per cent to the cost of the transcontinental road. Let it get on with the work and get it done. Some hon. members from the west have recommended that we have two transcontinental highways, and some of them have suggested feeder lines going from the south to the north, and from the north to the south from this transcontinental road. I say let us forget all this for the time being. Let us set our sights on the transcontinental highway. Let the government pay an appreciable share of the cost. Let us get on with the work and get it done; let us have one highway completed as soon as we possibly can so we can travel from east to west and west to east and enjoy the scenery which is ours.
I could not help but notice the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River about the specifications for this road. I was wondering whether the road would stand up to the traffic, when we realize there are tractor trailers using our highways at the present time and carrying 30, 34 and 35 tons of freight. Now is the time to take a second look at this bill; now is the time to'make this road adequate for the needs of the Canadian public, not for now but for 20 or 30 years from now.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a few brief remarks to make on this occasion. I did not take part in the debate earlier because I felt there were members present who were more familiar with this bill. But in listening to the debate so far it has seemed to me that though this bill provides for some acceleration in the construction of the trans-Canada highway, it is certainly not the answer to the kind of speeches that have been made from all sides of the house in this debate.
As I listened to the debate at the resolution stage I was perhaps unduly encouraged by the vision and spirit that was being manifested on all sides of the house, and particularly on this side of the house, as to the possibilities that lay before our nation if we had a proper network of highways. We have now come to the bill itself and we find, of course, it is a very narrow bill that deals only with the completion of the trans-Canada highway and does not take into consideration many of the objectives which have been expressed by speakers during the debate.
There is one particular part of the bill which is interesting to me because it may involve a change of policy. I do not know whether or not it does involve a change, but I should like to raise that question at this time in order that the minister may reply to it later if he so desires. I notice the bill provides that the Minister of Public Works is to be responsible for this act instead of the minister of resources and development. It so happens that in this case the minister is taking the act along with him into another department.
If that is the only object in that change, then perhaps no harm will be done. But if the change involves what it appears to involve, in that it takes away the idea of resources and development from the trans-Canada highway and makes it a straight public works proposition, then I for one would feel very disquieted because, as the hon. member for Bow River so ably stated in his address this afternoon, there are two particular objectives that can be served by a trans-Canada system.
I have used the word system rather than the words "trans-Canada highway", because it is my considered opinion that it will not be long before we shall feel the need of a trans-Canada highway system rather than just one road. I am very doubtful whether one trans-Canada highway from coast to coast will serve the needs of an expanding nation such as ours with its buoyant economy. The hon. member for Bow River mentioned the fact that there are two aspects of service in such a highway system; that is, the commercial and the recreational aspect. My contention is that
Trans-Canada Highway Act both are equally important. It is also my contention that no single route can hope to serve both these objectives.
I realize that the provincial governments perhaps had more to do with the choosing of the route of the highway than had the federal government; therefore I am not being critical of this government for the route that has been chosen. In my opinion, however, the route that is now being followed, through the prairie provinces at least, is the most uninteresting part of the provinces through which a tourist may hope to travel. I say this with all due respect to that part of my own province of Manitoba which I know is dear to the hearts of those hon. members who have constituencies along that highway.
So far as the commercial objective is concerned I would say the highway follows an excellent route in that province, but certainly from a tourist's point of view anyone who is familiar with the province of Manitoba will know that the scenic beauty and recreational interests of the province start a considerable distance north of the present highway route. It misses entirely, for example, Riding Mountain national park which is one of the greatest national parks in this country. It misses many other scenic areas in the northern part of the province which are developing quickly at the present time.
Even from a commercial point of view it can easily be seen that if a loop of the highway system were to pass through northern and western Manitoba and go as far north as Flin Flon, then link up with Nipawin, Saskatchewan and carry on through that province, in addition to passing through some of the most wonderful tourist country in Canada it would be useful in opening up valuable mining districts which today are served only by railway and in some cases are not served by transportation at all.
In my opinion attention has to be paid in the very near future to enlarging the concept of the trans-Canada highway to a trans-Canada highway system. There will be areas in which the commercial and tourist objectives can be synchronized along one route. That may be true to some extent in the province of Ontario, but certainly once you hit the prairies where you find the population spread over a much larger area to the north and south than is the case in Ontario, you can see immediately that one route will not adequately serve either the commercial or recreational objective of this highway system.
Apart from these considerations I for one am very glad the government has gone this far at least. The adequacy of the provisions of this bill have been thoroughly discussed
30S6	HOUSE OF
Trans-Canada Highway Act by previous speakers, and I need not add my comments. I am glad the government has at least gone this far in helping what we hope will be the acceleration of the completion of this highway.
At times I have felt quite embarrassed, and I am sure we have all had that experience, in travelling between eastern and western Canada in that we have to pass through the United States because of their splendid highways. It is not that we have anything against the United States; it is a fine country and its inhabitants are fine people. It does seem a bit of a national embarrassment, however, that in a country as beautiful as ours we have to by-pass what is from a tourist's point of view perhaps the most beautiful part of a trip between, let us say, Montreal and Winnipeg, and go around on the south side of the great lakes in order to stay on good roads. That is one aspect of the matter. I believe it would be a good thing for us if we could travel across Canada from coast to coast, and we hope to see that accomplished in the future.
There is also another aspect of the matter. We talk about tourist trade, and we go to quite an expense and a great deal of trouble in advertising Canadian tourist attractions in the United States and even further south in Mexico and other countries, endeavouring to sell our tourist attractions to foreign nations, which is a good thing. Unfortunately we do not get as much benefit from that as we would if we had a good highway system. One matter we overlook, and I think this is our greatest loss from the point of view of the tourist, is that we are unable to attract Canadian tourists, for example, from eastern Canada or the eastern coast to the western coast and vice versa. This is not necessarily a loss in dollars and cents, but I think we are missing an opportunity in this field.
In this house and in the provincial legislatures we talk a great deal about national unity, about building up a pride in our country and building up a feeling of belonging, of citizenship and patriotism. This is all to the good. I would point out, however, that one trip through Canada from coast to coast on a good highway would do more for the average person than 200 speeches in the House of Commons on the subject of citizenship, patriotism and love of our country. One has to see to believe and to truly appreciate.
I think it represents a national loss which cannot be measured in dollars and cents when many hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens who are travelling from east to west or from west to east each year must pass through the United States in order to


reach their destinations. That is one thing I think we should bear in mind when considering this bill.
I believe it should be emphasized that our highway system is needed not only from commercial and recreational points of view but because it would form part of our national defence system. Recently conferences have been held across Canada in connection with civil defence. I have read reports of those conferences, as no doubt other hon. members have, and one of the things that struck me has been that civil defence co-ordinators, local captains and so on, who are concerned with this phase of our activity, have stated that from the national and civil defence point of view our present transportation facilities are shockingly inadequate.
It has been said that if there were a crisis- it does not necessarily have to be war; it could be some other form of crisis which would be just as serious as war-we would find a great number of bottlenecks in our transportation system which would prove to be most serious. As reference has been made to bottlenecks I want to take advantage of this opportunity to refer to what was said the other day about Winnipeg being a bottleneck in transportation to western Canada. I do not like that term being applied to the city of Winnipeg, which we regard as the gateway to the west. I particularly do not like that term bottleneck being applied at this time in view of the excitement which is taking place in our province in connection with beer and liquor. I hope that term will not be used until after this issue has been settled in the city of Winnipeg.
I do not wish to hold up the house any longer. I have expressed a few thoughts. I hope that apart altogether from the provisions of this bill this parliament will not long delay giving attention to the provision of an adequate trans-Canada highway system which will serve the country from the point of view of commercial, recreational and civil defence needs.

Judging from the amount of construction completed to the present date and using the number of years from 1949 to 1956 as some sort of measuring rod, I am afraid the government will be compelled to extend still further into the future the completion of the first national highway in Canada.
I believe the situation is becoming scandalous. Let me point out that last year a program of highway building costing federal and state governments over $101 billion for the next ten years was adopted by the Eisenhower administration.

speechtext:
In Canada we are still waiting for the completion of our first trans-Canada highway. I say we should be thinking in terms of not one trans-Canada highway but numerous trans-Canada highways, and the time of commencement of these should be now. I think the situation in our country is that we are too retarded in our thinking on this important subject.
On numerous occasions in the past I have stressed the urgency of undertaking such a program. In this connection I urged in previous debates that a department of roads be set up to accomplish this objective. Speaking for my own area in western Canada, I again suggest that a northerly east-west route from Winnipeg by way of Saskatoon, Edmonton, Jasper park and the Yellowhead route to the west coast merits immediate attention. I think the terrain along this route, the elevation and the snowfall conditions, lend themselves ideally to a super four-lane highway. Such a route would connect the industrial and developing areas of western Canada with the east.
There is something further I wish to mention. There is the matter of the urgency of defence considerations which I believe are involved in this matter of roads in our country. On many occasions we have heard desperate pleas from competent sources urging study of mass evacuation of our cities. I think we must try desperately to prevent such action from ever becoming a necessity; but


should the time ever come when it is necessary, how in the world can we possibly evacuate our cities unless we have proper roads and highways? I say to you that it would be monumental cruelty for us to continue procrastinating on this important subject.
I have in my hand an important article which has a significant message. It is taken from the New York Times of March 12, 1955. It is headed "Clay Backs System of Superhighways" and reads in part as follows:
Washington, March 11 (UP): Gen. Lucius D. Clay, retired, said today it would be "just about impossible" to evacuate United States cities in an atomic attack without a multi-billion dollar new system of interstate super-highways.
In a strong appeal to a Senate public works subcommittee he asserted that it would be the "greatest mistake we ever made" if congress failed to vote "roads for survival" . . .
He headed President Eisenhower's highway committee that recommended a 10-year, $101 billion road building program . . .
Gen. Clay agreed it would be "very difficult" to empty cities even with the proposed system. But he said a "many, many times better job" could be done. . . . He asserted, however, that "we could save many lives" by evacuating "secondary" areas tainted with radioactivity after a nuclear attack.
While we are appropriating again this year several billions of dollars for munitions and arms, we hand out a few peanuts to the provinces for roads which can serve defensive and peaceful purposes. Considering along the civil defence angle, it is not unreasonable for us to suggest that the federal government should provide substantially all the funds needed for modernizing a strategic network of highways in our country. I think the government would be right in breaking with its existing policies and thinking along the lines I have mentioned.
There are other reasons why the government ought to revise its thinking respecting highways and road construction in our dominion. We can hardly expect the respective provinces of Canada to continue shouldering the financial burden of building roads while the federal government reaps the colossal revenues derived from excise and sales taxes on vehicles and industries associated with roads. It is true that under our constitution the responsibility for building roads lies with the provinces. Let me point out, however, that aiding the provinces in their road programs would mean aiding provincial economies, which field is taxed heavily by the senior government.
The controversy that has been carried on in this house during the past two days over whose responsibility it is becomes a joke when one considers that the matter is linked with our national economy and our national defence.	-

I believe the verdict of the people of Canada would be for the calling of a conference of representatives of the various provincial governments to aid, and objectively formulate, a national highway program truly worthy of our great country. Such a request was made by Premier Manning of the province of Alberta as far back as March of 1953 and again on April 10, 1953. At that time he was acting in accordance with the wishes and with the consent of the governments of the three western provinces, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. I am sorry to say that nothing came of those requests for such a meeting. What we actually need are less words and misunderstanding and a little more action and performance.

Mr. Speaker, one thing we are quite sure of by now is that there is a considerable difference of opinion about the condition of the roads in this country. I am a little worried about speaking today after that lecture the hon. member for Broadview received earlier. Though I did not take part in this debate at the resolution stage, I have gone to the trouble to see if I have ever said anything like this in past years, so I think I can be reasonably clear that I am not going to be guilty of any repetition in so far as this debate is concerned.
One of the things that depresses me about this subject was something I recall was stated by the Conservative member for Queens (Mr. MacLean). I think he referred to an Indian potentate in his example, but it amounted to this, that you can go broke buying bargains. It appears to me that that type of solution is being offered by this government to the various provinces. There is not very much point in suggesting that we are going to be prepared here to match a certain number of dollars when those dollars in fact do not exist.
I might refer specifically to the remarks by the hon. member for York Centre. Of all the people in this house I think he is quite well aware of the restrictions in connection with municipal and provincial financing. He was a member of the municipal council in his own district of York Centre. I think he must realize that although the province of Ontario may be showing a surplus in so far as its budget is concerned, it is building roads at an expanding and accelerating rate. I am afraid it is having to finance them on an amortization plan, which may cause us considerable heartache in the future. Yet if it does not do so the true seriousness of the situation is going to be reflected in the fact that many other essential services such as
Trans-Canada Highway Act the building of schools may be affected. I am not going any further with my remarks in that connection because I can almost see you ready to rise, Mr. Speaker, and say that at this point I am out of order.
However, the provincial situation is such that no matter what province it may be, the continuing financial strain is almost getting to the breaking point. I say to hon. members of this house that that is just as applicable to the so-called rich province of Ontario as it is to any of those that might consider themselves less fortunate.
I listened to the hon. member for Fort William. I respect his opinion and I like to talk to him regularly, but when he says we have had remarkable leadership in this connection, I think he is far off the mark. As a matter of fact the chief thing that is the matter with this particular program is that there is no pioneering spirit being shown in it. When we try to compare this with the building of the C.P.R. in the early days of confederation, the two just do not go together. At that time there was a spirit throughout this land which was fostered by the people in charge of the government at that time, and which ensured that that very necessary railway was built and apparently built just as quickly as we are going to have this trans-Canada highway built in the years to follow.
I should like to say that in the last six months I have seen some road construction in Mexico. Taking a look at the time that is involved, I believe that road construction in Mexico is going on just as quickly as on this trans-Canada highway. It is being done with picks and shovels and without any of the automatic equipment that we have to carry out the construction program here in Canada. It is a sad state of affairs when lands of that type, building in country just as difficult as our own, are able to keep up to us with the use of picks and shovels.
I have seen some of the trans-Canada highway, and I might say I have seen a part in the riding of the hon. member for Bow River. When I saw it I thought you could use it as a pedestrian way if you wore hip boots, but from the standpoint of using it as a highway, it is going to be many years, if we continue the present pace, before it will be in use for the moving of people and goods.
