I said the other night that the government can always find an excuse for not going ahead. They can tell us about provincial rights, but when they find something for their own political purposes they can forget them very easily. I say this

Trans-Canada Highway Act is one of the occasions when they might get down off the pinnacle and deal with the people at the level at which we can accomplish something. I do not think they should tell us they have no money. No, sir; they have the money, all right. They collected it from the people to whom it should be returned in the form of highways which will be of some benefit to the whole country.
At this point I am going to say I am repeating, because I used these figures once before, but I think they can bear repetition. According to the public accounts of Canada, volume I, for the year 1954, this government collected $94,715,040 in excise taxes on automobiles. It collected $11,381,716 in taxes on rubber tires, tubes and articles of that kind. From figures it is almost impossible for me to calculate the amount of sales tax, but the Canadian Automobile Association presented a brief to the Minister of Finance on September 10, 1954, and their estimate was that the government also collected approximately $90 million in sales tax. In addition the government has collected on an annual basis somewhere between $25 million and $50 million of taxes on imported vehicles.
I am not going to refer to the tremendous amount of corporation tax which has been collected from the automobile companies, but obviously that tax in fact is paid by the consumer, the person who buys the cars and trucks. How many millions of dollars it is I would not even dare estimate. But even the figures I have given you here today, sir, indicate that approximately $250 million can be collected in this manner annually. What did this government do for the people who paid this tax? Well, I will tell you. In that year they spent $13,378,998 on the trans-Canada highway. At the same time it cost about $400,000 for the administration of that highway, and I think they spent about $750,000 on the parkway system in the Ottawa area, so all told it was something like $14 million or $15 million.
Now, sir, they are collecting $250 million annually and they are spending for the motorist, for the person who buys the trucks and cars, approximately $14 million or $15 million. As a matter of fact they collect enough in a year to cover the total expenditure that I heard read out Dy the minister since the inception of this program. One years' collection of taxes from these people would pay the complete cost of this particular highway so far. It is high time, sir, that this type of taxation was used for the benefit of the people who pay it. As long as we continue to have this type of taxation, as long as there is no responsibility to plow it back into the facilities that are required by the


people who pay the tax, so long you are going to continue to have this type of headline: "Frost Asks $100 Million More". Why does he ask that? Because this government does not put it back where it belongs; and so long as it continues that policy so long will every province of this dominion require a greater amount of money from the federal treasury.
There is only one other item I should like to speak about. You know, sir, since I have been moved over to this area I have had a couple of letters from people congratulating me on being appointed parliamentary assistant to the hon. member for the Yukon. As a matter of fact I cannot think of anyone better to be parliamentary assistant to. When I heard him speak the other night about the problems of the Yukon and of the Northwest Territories and of the access roads that are required to the coast I thought it would be a wonderful thing if hon. members here could see some of the roads out there and see some of the country out there. I have seen it, and I was very much impressed with it. It is a long way from York West to the northwest, but it was a wonderful experience.
It seems to me that at this time-and I shall relate these remarks to the trans-Canada highway and the trans-Canada highway system-when the natural resources of this country are so much in demand by our friends to the south and when I would venture to say that the demand for those resources is going to increase, it is a wonderful opportunity for this country to bargain from strength for the privileges the hon. member for Yukon spoke about the other day in the budget debate.
The minister has said that we in this house are responsible for the operation of the highways in Yukon and the Northwest Territories. There is no question about that, or about our having to share that responsibility with anybody else. It boils right down to us. It seems to me that if we are to develop the north, sir, one of the things we should be aiming for is an integration of the highways in that northwest area with this trans-Canada highway system. If I can make any plea in this house today for the future of the northwest it would be that we heed very much the warning of the hon. member for Yukon and see whether we cannot integrate that highway system with the trans-Canada highway system, and whether we cannot bargain from strength to obtain the corridors required to ensure that we open up those areas.

Mr. Speaker, probably what I have to say will be ruled out of order with the statement that the remarks of the hon. member for Vegre-ville were out of order. The hon. member was permitted to put on the record some editorials which gave just about as thoroughly a distorted view of the highway situation in Alberta as any editorials possibly could. I should like to take just a few minutes to set before the house and the country the facts
Trans-Canada Highway Act pertaining to the situation in Alberta. I hope I can do this in five or ten minutes without being called to order.
Nothing has been said by any of these newspapers which were quoted by any of these brilliant Liberals who come down here to kick their own province in the face about the fact that in 1935 there were 80,000 miles of road to be built in Alberta, and that at that time there was not one single mile of graded and paved road in that province. The territory which had to be served by those 80,000 miles of road was settled almost all over because of the peculiarities of the settlement of Alberta. There were great areas along the Canadian Pacific railway and great areas owned by the Hudson's Bay Company and other concerns which resulted in the spreading of population all over the province.
The result was that these roads had to be built. The people in all these areas were clamouring for roads; they needed them. Any government which in 1935 undertook to build a road system that was suitable for Alberta could not afford to spend all its money on a few hundred miles of road and leave the rest of the 80,000 miles unserviced. They simply had to spread out their money and their work, which meant that no single mile of road in Alberta could possibly be up to the high standard which might be prescribed. They had to build the best they could, realizing that a tremendous area had to be covered. It was something like a man with 15 children who all needed shoes. He could not buy every one of those children a pair of shoes costing $15; probably he would have to get them shoes costing $3 or else buy them moccasins.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the bones of contention among hon. members as they have talked to each other across the floor ever since this measure began to be considered has been whether or not the provinces should bear a more generous share of the cost of the trans-Canada highway or whether the dominion should. I think each province has particular difficulties which give it just about all the troubles it can bear. I was on the point of mentioning some of those difficulties as regards Alberta to show that she certainly is not in a position to spend any more money on the trans-Canada highway than she absolutely has to spend.
I mentioned before the house took recess that we had 80,000 miles of road to build in Alberta; that with a population spread over so large a part of the province there was a great demand for roads in nearly every part of it. I should like to draw attention to two or three other aspects of our provincial situation which are disregarded by many of our Alberta Liberal members who come down here and report about the province.
In the first place, Alberta is a foothill province. I do not believe there is another area of land on the North 'American continent that has conditions identical with those of Alberta. Because of the fact that there are so many swamps, so many areas where drainage is sluggish and such a tendency for springs to come up in wet years, we frequently build first-class roads over a certain area never dreaming that there are springs under those roads. Then when a very wet year comes along we have springs coming up right in the middle of the roads. We have had that happen in a good many cases. We have had to dig down 15, 16 or more feet because of the deterioration before we could build another road over the top.
Things like that need to be borne in mind in dealing with Alberta. Because of the fact that she is a foothill province she is very different from other provinces. Consequently when the engineers went to work planning roads in Alberta they had nothing to go by, and although we had the very best engineers we could obtain there had to be a good deal of experimentation which resulted in losses of roads and great additional costs.
There is another important matter which indicates the difficulty that Alberta has. That is the great variety of climate. Sometimes we have very wet years and sometimes we have four, five, or even ten dry years. People


would become accustomed to the dry years and build a road where they thought it would certainly be secure and safe, but lo and behold when a wet year came it was anything but secure and safe. There was always the danger of having roads heave in the wintertime as the result of frost, especially if we had wet falls.
When the hon. member for Vegreville read the editorials from those two papers he made no mention of facts like these. The two editorials made no mention of these facts, and if they were going to be fair they should have done so. It needs to be borne in mind that every mile of road in Alberta from the time Social Credit took over in 1935 was built under the direction of the very best engineering advice that could be obtained. I will challenge anyone to show wherein that was not true, or wherein there was any wastefulness or inefficiency in building roads. The simple fact is that roads did not stand up because of the reasons I have given, and we had to build roads over again.
There is another most pertinent thing. The important major oil discovery in Alberta was in the Leduc field in 1947. Roads which stood up to the traffic in Alberta up to 1947 simply were hopelessly inadequate when the great machines and the great trucks laden with very heavy oil equipment and machines started to travel over those roads in great numbers. Consequently nearly all the north and south roads which we had and which we thought would stand up were simply destroyed by the tremendous traffic over them from 1947 and 1948 onward especially in wet years.
There is another thing that has to be borne in mind. In addition to the great number of roads we had to build, our revenues were very meagre. The first Social Credit budget in 1936,1 believe, was in the neighbourhood of $15 million. When you bear in mind that practically 49 cents out of every single dollar of revenue that was acquired had to go for the payment of interest on bonds alone you can see the conditions under which the government laboured when it endeavoured to provide roads in a province like that with the conditions I have already mentioned.
I do not think I need to say anything more, Mr. Speaker. Anyone who is realistic, anyone who is inclined to be honest and fair, will realize that under the circumstances editorials like those read by the hon. member for Vegreville were published by papers that did not intend in any way to be fair. They were deliberately trying to hurt the province and deliberately trying to hurt the government of that province which, as I have said in times past, is in my opinion the finest government

that is to be found on the North American continent, if not in the whole world. All we desire is that men tell the truth about us, and give us a chance to go on and do in the future work comparable with what has been done in the past.
What I have said certainly indicates to the minister that we have no money to spend on the trans-Canada highway other than what we absolutely have to spend. Yet Alberta has, I believe, built her share of the trans-Canada highway-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-right up to date and has in many cases built far ahead of the money the minister has paid. In other words, I am told that she has built sections of the road and has had to wait six, seven or eight months before receiving the dominion's share.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to make these few observations. I think my hon. friends from Alberta will find what I have said completely unanswerable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two Questions that I should perhaps answer in winding up the debate at this stage. The hon. member for Broadview spoke today in the capacity of official critic for the official opposition. Therefore I would imagine that the views he expressed were those that the Progressive Conservative party wish to convey on the measure before the house at the present time. I rather gathered that he is under some misapprehension as to the role of the federal government in the trans-Canada highway and the relationship between the provinces and the federal government with respect to this project.
This all came about, as I said in my statement, because of what seemed to be the wish of the provincial governments and on the part of the public generally to have the federal government provide some financing and to co-ordinate the project, but it was never suggested by anybody responsible that the federal government should insert itself into the prior position, that it should assume any responsibility for ownership of the highway or that it should contribute toward maintenance once the highway was completed. The concept was to join up ten provincial roads to form a trans-Canada highway; and since that had some national complexion the federal government was justified in participating, but only on the grounds that the provincial autonomy would be protected at all times, that the highway would be constructed
Trans-Canada Highway Act By the provincial governments, and that provincial practices as to highway construction would be adhered to to the greatest possible extent.
The hon. member talked about the limitation of federal funds on the rate of construction of the trans-Canada highway. I do not think that is a correct concept. At no time have the federal funds voted by this parliament been a deterrent or a limiting factor on the pace of construction of the trans-Canada highway. The money has been available, and we would have been gratified had the pace proceeded faster than it did. Our mutual regret-and when I say "mutual" I mean the provinces and ourselves-is that they have not been able to do as much work as they contemplated originally for reasons which I gave this afternoon when I opened this debate on second reading. The provinces themselves have never suggested or asked that we take over ownership of this highway or assist with the maintenance of it. Those were clear understandings from the start.
I referred to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I said that extremely important project took 11 years to complete. I also said that if this measure is passed, parliament will be providing 11 years in which to complete the trans-Canada highway. When we view this present project in the light of present-day techniques and construction methods I think 11 years for a trans-Canada highway is far more than was comparable when the C.P.R. was built. The impression I intended to convey was that if the C.P.R. could be built in the last century in 11 years, then surely with the nine provinces working together and with the financial assistance and the co-ordination of the federal government, we should be able to build a trans-Canada highway in less time than that.
I wish to make one more reference to that matter. The hon. member said the C.P.R. was built smoothly, efficiently and without any difficulties at all.

subsubtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext: No; I did not say "without difficulties". I said "smoothly and efficiently".

subsubtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
As reference reading I would commend to the hon. member "The Old Chieftain", which is a very good book and which gives a clear picture of the difficulties and some of the other problems encountered in the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
This whole operation as envisaged by the bill now before us is a gap-closing operation. I say that now for the benefit of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). Later on I shall have cause to deal with some of the other remarks he made. It is not

Trans-Canada Highway Act intended to be an invasion of provincial juris1 diction, as some of the remarks made by hon. members of the opposition would seem to be inviting the federal government to undertake.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) was concerned primarily about the standards of the trans-Canada highway. I should say to him that the specification was a matter of agreement. From the outset we have said that we would be guided by provincial practices so long as the ultimate requirements are met. The hon. member stated that the base course set out in the agreement is not adequate. Actually there is no dimension specified for the thickness of the base course. The specification requires that the road shall be built to carry an axle loading of 18,000 pounds. I know of no province in Canada that specifies a load-carrying capacity greater than that. The method to achieve that load-carrying capacity is up to the provincial government. If the aggregate or granular material available in any one area requires a greater thickness than that- if it requires a 2-foot thickness-it is up to the provincial government to specify the thickness of a base course that will provide the load-carrying capacity set out in the agreement.
The hon. member mentioned the thickness of the asphalt and rather implied that it is limited to 3 inches. Actually the specification states that it shall be 3 inches, but there is no reason why it should not be more than that. We have actually approved and paid for a greater thickness than 3 inches. We have accepted and paid for a thickness up to 5 inches.
In Alberta as in some other provinces there is an asphalt stabilized base course which is usually something of the order of three inches thick and sometimes thicker, so that the total asphalt is usually at least six inches, with three inches top asphalt and three inches stabilized base course.

subsubtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext: Do you think that is thick enough to carry the traffic?

subsubtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext: Schedule B that is before the provincial governments now will specify 3 inches as a minimum. I think trans-Canada highway specifications have helped to set the standards in Alberta and elsewhere. It was on the trans-Canada highway in Alberta that the first shoulders were paved. My hon. friend made quite a point of that fact this afternoon. He referred to the matter of the right of way and deplored that it should be limited to 100 feet. The 100 feet width is specified as the minimum. As the provinces acquire and pay for the right of way, they are of course free to acquire any width they wish.

speechtext: That would be an additional expense to the province not shared by the federal government.

subsubtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
That is right; the provincial government is required to acquire and pay for the right of way.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) deplored the lack of progress at Banff and said there is not any mileage completed. There are some reasons for that fact. I assured the hon. member this afternoon that this highway would be completed within the period now set in this legislation. But there is one thing that I think I should, in all fairness, point out. That is that there are 37 miles of paved highway from the east gate at Banff to lake Louise. That had been the route of the trans-Canada highway until 1954 when it was decided to go south of the Bow river, so we have an entirely new route. We chose it in 1954, as I said, and we have already awarded contracts for grading along that route and in fact we have now under contract the grading of some 61-4 miles along the route of the trans-Canada highway in Banff and Yoho national parks.
The hon. member for Algoma West (Mr. Nixon) asked me three questions about the route of the highway in western Ontario. He asked: Before the location of the trans-Canada highway can be determined, must it be referred to the federal government? The answer of course is yes. He asked: Has the route through Sault Ste. Marie been requested by the government of Ontario? Today I received a letter from the minister of highways of the province of Ontario. It is dated April 17. They wish to build two roads in that area, one north from Thessalon and the other north from Sault Ste. Marie. They will of course ask for federal participation with respect to only one of the roads. The road now delineated in the schedule to the present agreement is from Sudbury to Chap-leau. The road will either follow approximately the route of the Canadian Pacific Railway or will follow an alternate route via Thessalon, Ontario, depending on surveys yet to be made.
The Ontario government is now contemplating, and has asked for approval of, a route from Sudbury to follow highway No. 17 to Thessalon, continue along highway No. 17 to Sault Ste. Marie and then continue along highway No. 17 northerly from the Sault to the end of the presently constructed highway at Agawa, then to follow the surveyed location from Agawa northerly to Michipicoten, White River, Marathon and Schreiber. If that is the route the Ontario government requests, we shall certainly be pleased to give it favourable consideration.

The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) said we should participate in the cost of climbing lanes for trucks, and he quoted an example. In that particular illustration, he was under the impression that the federal government did not contribute, whereas actually we did pay one-half the cost of the climbing lanes as well as our share of the other costs of the road, and that is provided for under the terms of the agreement.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said that this should be an effort to close the gaps. With that, of course, we are all in agreement. The whole object of this exercise is to make an assault on these gaps, so as to enable people to travel in comfort by vehicle from one coast of Canada to the other. The remaining gaps are in Ontario and in Newfoundland. There is a 135-mile gap in Ontario between the Agawa river and a point east of Marathon, assuming the route chosen is the one through Sault Ste. Marie to which I have just referred. In Newfoundland there is a 50-mile gap between Clarenville and Gambo. Those gaps are shorter than the mileages to which my hon. friend referred this afternoon. As he pointed out, his figures were the mileage as of March 31, 1955, whereas I am speaking of gaps obtaining at the present moment.
I do not think it is asking too much of the provinces collectively, with the measure of assistance that is being provided by the federal government, to build a trans-Canada highway in the period now being sought in this legislation before parliament. I should hope it could have the support of all hon. members. On this point, however, there are some doubts in my mind.
The hon. member for Broadview, who was speaking on behalf of the official opposition, although he was quite critical of the federal government's role in the development of the trans-Canada highway, did not criticize the role of the provincial governments despite the fact that one of the gaps in the highway is in his own province. He did not say whether he was for or against the legislation.
He was followed by four other spokesmen from the Progressive Conservative party, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stanton), the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton), the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, none of whom gave any indication of their attitude or that of their party with respect to this legislation.
There were three speakers from the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Bow River, the hon. member for Cariboo and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), and none of them gave any indication of whether 67509-196
Trans-Canada Highway Act they support this measure, which is designed . to accelerate the construction of a highway across Canada. The only member who indicated that he intended to support the legislation was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I think the country and the house have a right to know where hon. members stand on this legislation. I therefore ask you, Mr. Speaker if you would be kind enough, when putting the vote, to call for the yeas and the nays.

However, I have noticed that since that time, the government of the province of Quebec, on grounds of autonomy that I cannot understand, rejects all grants, although the people of the province of Quebec have to pay 2 cents 67509-197
Trans-Canada Highway Act more than their neighbours of Ontafio for each gallon of gasoline they use.
Recently I travelled over that highway from Levis to Montreal, and found it in poor condition. In fact, on at least half the distance it is a gravel road or a partly paved road. I noticed, particularly in Lotbiniere county, stacks of heavy wire which was meant to be used as concrete reinforcement on that highway which was never completed. And I could not help thinking that these were the skeletons of the lack of co-operation between the present government of the province of Quebec and the federal government.
I wish that instead of telling Mr. Duplessis unkind things about his lack of co-operation, Quebec members of the opposition had at least pointed out to him the urgency of putting an end to his obstruction so that, at last, our province might have that highway for the building of which we are paying taxes while millions of dollars offered for that purpose by the federal government are being stubbornly refused.

I understand also that this lack of cooperation comes from the fact that, in some provinces and particularly in ours, the governments do not like to award contracts to the lowest bidder. Trans-Canada Highway Act lethargy and decides to set an example to the provinces in getting this highway built by at least completing its meagre 83 miles in the national parks, and when we finally get this national highway built, it will give serious consideration to two things; one, participating with the provinces in properly maintaining this highway and not just handing it over to the provinces and leaving it to them; two, the building of a second route in the west from Saskatoon to Edmonton and on to the coast, which is badly needed.
Also, as the hon. member for Kamloops has suggested, once this national highway has been built and a possible second route built, I hope this government will give serious consideration to undertaking a national highway program. As one hon. member has just correctly suggested, this government will not be the government then. That is quite right. I hope the government of that time will give serious consideration to a national highway program in conjunction with the provinces which will open up our country and develop our tourist trade and our national resources, and make it possible to man adequately our defences.
Since the federal government will be the main beneficiary of the revenue which will accrue from the development of our national resources and our tourist industry through the medium of sales taxes and corporation taxes, there should be no reluctance on the part of the government to participate in such a program. Since our national defence is solely a federal responsibility, there should certainly be no reluctance on the part of the federal government to participate in the building of such highways.
I believe such a program should be considered an investment in Canada's future, an investment in our national development, and that it should not be paid for out of current revenue but by the issuing of long-term bonds. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is substantially the amendment that was moved when the resolution was being considered, and I was obliged at that time to say that the government could not accept it. My position is the same tonight. Under the legislation, and the agreement which will be pursuant thereto, it will be the prior role of the provincial governments to choose the locations they wish to have considered for the application of the gap formula; but their selection will of course be subject to the approval of the federal government. I do not expect that there will be any matters of great disagreement between the provincial governments and the federal government in the determination of the locations. I think the section as it stands gives the federal government no more than a proper opportunity to exercise the authority that I believe the taxpayers would expect it to exercise when dealing with amounts of money of the magnitude contemplated by this bill. The government is therefore unable to accept the amendment moved by the hon. member for Broadview.

subsubtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the facility with which this government and the minister dodge from position to position is extraordinary. The minister takes the position on the one hand that the federal government is to be given credit for the fact that they conceived the idea of the trans-Canada highway program. Then when we say to him: "Well, why do you not get on with it?" he says, "Of course we can do nothing because the main responsibility for roads is with the provinces". Then we say to him, "But you have said that there is difficulty in getting the provinces to do what they should. We have explained to you why they cannot get on any faster than they are with the building, and we suggest that you assume a greater responsibility". Then he says, "No, we cannot do that. All we can do is call a conference of the provinces". He tells us of the number of conferences they have had and the efforts they have made to spur the provinces on to greater activity. He told us that this afternoon.

We now say, "All right; if that is your position and if this thing is a provincial responsibility, then give the provinces the right to determine what would be to their greatest advantage with respect to the selection of the route on which you now give them 90 per cent assistance". Then he turns around and says, "No, we cannot do that because the responsibility in this matter is that of the federal government". Which position is the minister going to take?
If in fact what is to be done is to give the provinces the opportunity and the encouragement to get on with this construction, why does he not do it? If on the other hand he is not going to give them that opportunity, why does he not take the other course we urge him to take and say that the federal government should have the full responsibility for this highway and not a paltry 10 per cent of its length? The minister is trying to straddle both positions and he is going to find, just as we forecast when this trans-Canada proposal first came up and we said it could not be completed within the time that was then set, that his present position of blowing hot and cold on the question of whose responsibility it is, and this refusal on his part to give the provinces the responsibility to get on with the job, will result in the trans-Canada highway not being finished by December 31, 1960, either.
If the minister conscientiously takes the position he has now taken that this is a matter where the dominion must keep control, that he cannot trust the provinces and cannot allow them to say which 10 per cent they will select for the receipt of 90 per cent assistance, then let him follow up the logic of that position and say, "Very well, the dominion government will assume responsibility for the whole thing".
I ask hon. gentlemen opposite who are going to be asked to make up their minds and vote on this amendment now before us which position they want to take. Do they want to take the position that it is a federal responsibility or a provincial responsibility? So far the theme of the minister's speech is that it is a provincial responsibility. If that is the case we urge hon. members opposite to be logical and support the amendment, and not find themselves placed in the hopeless and inconsistent position in which they would be placed if they were to follow the minister's lead and vote against the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in listening to the discussion this evening, in so far as irresponsibility is concerned the ones who would appear to me to be irresponsible 67509-1974
Trans-Canada Highway Act are those who are suggesting the expenditure of additional funds which belong to the taxpayers of this country.
It is quite obvious to me that if any one of the ten provinces of Canada can make an agreement with this government whereby they have to pay only 10 per cent of the cost of any road, they will use every means in the world to have that road go just as far as possible. That is human nature. I believe that the stand taken by the minister is a most reasonable one. I have heard one suggestion made by an hon. member who spoke tonight. He suggested that the government did not allow sufficient time in which to complete the road. A few minutes later another hon. member of the same group suggested that the government wanted to delay the matter as long as possible. It would therefore appear that they do not get together in their arguments.
I for one feel we have a responsibility here as federal members. These fabulous suggestions as to the spending of the taxpayers' dollars must have some consideration. The hon. member who suggested that the federal government should pay the complete cost of the trans-Canada highway will be out on an economy program in the next election campaign. It does not make sense to me. I believe that we as federal members have a responsibility in this matter, and I believe we should not be spending the taxpayers' dollars any more freely than the provincial legislatures wish to spend theirs.

I should like to have some clarification as to how this clause will apply to Prince Edward Island, as I believe the application to that province might be slightly different from the application to other provinces due to the fact that the length of the highway in our province is so short. The total length of highway in Prince Edward Island is 74 miles and one-tenth of that would be 7-4 miles. That would mean that there could be only one gap in Prince Edward Island to which this 90 per cent formula could be applied, since a gap must be at least 5 miles in length. There being only 7-4 miles altogether that would mean that in the case of Prince Edward Island there would be one gap the length of which would be 7-4 miles. There would not be adequate mileage to allow for two gaps of 5 miles each.
That being the case, and in order that the intention of the amendment might be more properly understood as it applies to Prince Edward Island, I wonder if the minister would consider a slight amendment to paragraph (b) of subclause 2, and instead of the third line which reads:
-but any portion of the highway taken into account for the purposes of this paragraph shall be at least 5 miles in length.
I would suggest an amendment reading something like this:
-but not more than one portion of the highway taken into account for the purpose of this paragraph shall be less than 5 miles in length.

That formula would give Prince Edward Island an opportunity to apply the principle to one section which would be 5 miles in length and to another gap which would take up the remainder of the 10 per cent of the total mileage.
